question: I feel drawn to two creative directions. What can I compare without treating cards as a verdict?

output.directAnswer: You can compare the two creative directions by treating this card as a prompt about design, strategy, and execution—not as a verdict about which path is “right.” For each direction, make the plan visible: what are you trying to create, what assumptions does it depend on, what resources and commitments are required, and what would count as an early sign of progress? Also examine whether you are avoiding a difficult conversation, withholding relevant information, or trying to carry too many elements at once. A small, time-limited experiment for each direction can provide evidence without requiring a permanent choice. The card cannot determine an outcome, disclose hidden facts, or replace your judgment.

cards.interpretation: Visual observation: a walking man carries five swords while stepping away, looking back toward two swords left planted; an encampment and distant group appear behind him. In Waite’s recorded claims, the card includes design, attempt, wish, hope, confidence, quarrelling, and the possibility that a plan may fail. Editorially, this supports comparing the architecture of each creative direction and the honesty and practicality of its execution. Ask which option has a clearer design, what you may be leaving unresolved, and whether your strategy is sustainable rather than merely appealing. This is a symbolic lens, not evidence that either direction will succeed or fail.

realityChecks: Write a one-page brief for each direction: audience, intended result, next three actions, time available, cost or resources, and a testable milestone.
Run comparable small experiments—such as a prototype, sketch series, or short release—using the same evaluation period.
Record observable feedback: completion time, energy required, audience response, learning gained, and whether the work remains meaningful after the initial excitement.
Identify any conversations, permissions, collaborators, or commitments that must be handled openly before proceeding.
unknowns: The reading does not show which direction has better market, personal, or practical prospects.
It does not establish your available time, money, skills, collaborators, audience, or obligations.
It cannot reveal other people’s private intentions or guarantee how either experiment will be received.
Your priorities—such as income, freedom, mastery, recognition, or enjoyment—remain for you to define.
output.disclosure: This bounded interpretation uses only the immutable one-card reading provided: Seven of Swords upright in “What deserves attention,” from the accepted source projection. Waite’s claims are kept separate from visual observations and editorial interpretation. The card is used for reflection, while real-world evidence and your own decision-making remain decisive.
